title: Render to Caesar
subtitle: What a Christian owes the state, what a Christian owes God, and the difference that orders a whole life.

sections.title: The Coin and the Image
sections.body:
They came to trap him, and the trap was political. The Pharisees and the Herodians, two camps that agreed on almost nothing, agreed for one afternoon that Jesus had to be destroyed. Their question was a snare with teeth on both sides. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not. Say yes and you lose the crowd who hate Rome. Say no and you hand the soldiers a charge of sedition. There was no safe answer, only a choice of which enemy would take you. This is what political questions have always been. Not invitations to think but tests of loyalty, designed to sort you before you have spoken a full sentence.

He asked for a coin. He did not carry one. The denarius they produced bore the head of Tiberius and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, a small idol you could hold in your palm. Whose image is this, he asked, and whose inscription. Caesar's, they said. Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. The crowd heard a clever escape. What he actually said was a verdict that has outlasted the empire that minted the coin.

Here is the weight of it. The coin carries Caesar's image, so give the coin back to Caesar. It was his to begin with. But every person standing in that courtyard carried a different image, stamped not on metal but on the soul, and that image was not Caesar's. In the beginning God made man in his own image. The coin belongs to the state because the state's mark is on it. You belong to God because God's mark is on you. Jesus did not divide life into a sacred half and a secular half. He told them the state has real and limited claims, and God has a total one, and the second is the line the first may never cross.

This is the seed of everything that follows. The Christian gives the state taxes, obedience, honor, the labor of good citizenship, all of it freely. The Christian does not give the state worship, ultimate allegiance, or the conscience, because those were never the state's to ask for. We have spent centuries confusing the two ledgers. We render to Caesar things stamped with the image of God, and then wonder why our politics feels like idolatry. It feels that way because it is.

sections.title: Dual Citizenship
sections.body:
Paul wrote to a church in the capital of the empire and told them their citizenship was in heaven. He was not telling them to leave Rome. He himself used his Roman citizenship as a legal tool more than once, demanding the rights it gave him, appealing to Caesar when a lesser court would have killed him. The man who said our commonwealth is in heaven also said I appeal to Caesar. Both were true at once, and he felt no contradiction. He held two citizenships, and he knew the rank order between them.

The early Christians had a phrase for this. The letter to Diognetus, an early defense of the faith whose date is uncertain and commonly placed somewhere in the second or third century, described believers as people who live in their own countries but only as resident aliens. The paraphrase is faithful even if the wording here is not the ancient writer's exact phrasing. They marry, they pay taxes, they obey the laws, and they do all of it while belonging somewhere else first. They were not tourists who refused to invest in the place they lived. They were also not natives who mistook the place they lived for home. They paid in fully and they were owned by something the city could not see. That posture is the whole thing, and we keep collapsing it into one of two errors.

The first error is withdrawal. In its crude form it says the world is lost, politics is dirty, and the faithful thing is to pull back into a holy enclave and wait for the end. But withdrawal has a serious version that deserves a serious answer, and Rod Dreher named it the Benedict Option. It argues that the church has already lost the wider culture, that the more urgent task is to build communities thick enough to hand the faith intact to our children, and that a people with nothing to give cannot give anything to a nation. On that last point it is simply right. You cannot pour out what you have not first been formed to hold, and the church that skips formation for activism burns through its own children inside a generation. The error is not the call to form a people. The error is treating formation and presence as if you must choose. The resident alien is formed precisely so that he can stay, and a retreat that ends in abandonment is still abandonment, because your neighbor lives in the world you left, and the laws you ignore land on his body. The second error is takeover. It says if Christians simply seize enough power, pass enough laws, capture enough institutions, the kingdom will arrive by force. This sounds like courage. It is actually a loss of faith, because it trusts the sword to do what only the Spirit can do, and it always ends with the church looking exactly like the empire it set out to convert.

The resident alien refuses both. He does not withdraw, because he loves the city and seeks its welfare, as Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray for it. He does not seize, because he knows the city is not the kingdom and never will be. He works for justice without expecting justice to save him. He votes without believing the ballot is a sacrament. He grieves the country's sins as his own and serves its good as his calling, and underneath all of it he holds the quiet certainty that his deepest belonging is somewhere this election cannot reach. That certainty, far from detachment, is the very thing that makes durable engagement possible. You can only give yourself to a country with an open hand when you are sure of a country you cannot lose.

sections.title: How to Hold a Party
sections.body:
So vote. Engage. Run for the school board if you are called to it. The resident alien is not passive, and the New Testament never treats the governing of a society as beneath the believer. The question was never whether to participate. The question is how to participate without handing a political party the part of you that belongs to God. And the test is simple, almost embarrassingly so. Can you criticize your own side.

Watch how people talk and you will know who they actually worship. A person whose deepest loyalty is to God can name the failures of the party he votes for, can grieve when his own coalition lies or cruelly mistreats the weak, can refuse to defend the indefensible just because it wears his colors. A person whose deepest loyalty is to the party has lost this ability entirely. Every accusation against his side is a hoax, every leader on his side is a victim, every compromise of principle is actually wisdom when his people do it and treason when the others do. He has not chosen a party. He has been absorbed by one. The mark of the absorbed is that they can no longer be surprised by their own team, and they can no longer be honest about it.

The freedom Jesus gives is the freedom to hold the platform with an open hand, and that freedom is not a temperament. It is purchased. A person who has been crucified with Christ has already died, and the self that a party could threaten or flatter died with him. You cannot blackmail a dead man with the loss of his side, and you cannot buy a dead man with the win of it. Raised into a life that is hidden with Christ, he has nothing left for a coalition to seize, because the one thing that could be seized was surrendered at the cross before the first ballot was ever cast. The grip loosens because the grave already did its work. A party is a coalition, a temporary alliance of interests assembled to win, and no coalition has ever been the kingdom of God. So you can vote for one while seeing clearly what is wrong with it. You can pull a lever for the candidate who will, on balance, do less harm or more good, and walk out of the booth owing that candidate nothing, no defense, no spin, no silence about his sins. Far from lukewarm, this is the only kind of engagement that stays free. The person who cannot criticize his own side has already given that side his worship, and he gave away the one thing he was told to render to God alone.

There is a discipline here worth naming. The honest test of any political act is whether the same person would condemn the identical act if the other side committed it. When the answer is yes, the conscience has already rendered its verdict and partisanship is the thing overriding it, and that contradiction is an alarm whether or not a man lets himself hear it. The goal in all of this was never to stand above politics, floating in some false neutrality that is usually just cowardice in a clean shirt. The goal is to be in politics as a free person, owned by God, lending your strength to a cause without ever selling your soul to it.

sections.title: The Church Is Not a PAC
sections.body:
Here is the temptation that has hollowed out more congregations than any heresy. A church looks at the scale of the nation's problems, feels the genuine urgency of them, and decides that the most important thing it can do is to deliver votes. It becomes, in everything but name, a wing of a campaign. The sermons shift. The enemies become the same enemies the cable channel named on Tuesday. The pastor measures faithfulness by whether the right people won. And the strange thing is that this always feels like seriousness. It feels like the church finally engaging the real world. It is actually the church forgetting what it is for.

The church's first political act is not to lobby, fund, or mobilize. The church's first political act is to be the church. To be a community where the divisions that organize the rest of society simply do not hold. Where the rich and the poor sit at the same table and the same cup is passed to both. Where the immigrant and the native, the laborer and the executive, the person who voted one way and the person who voted the other, are bound together by something stronger than their disagreements, and stay bound when those disagreements are real and sharp. That community is itself a political statement, louder than any endorsement, because it shows the watching world an arrangement of human life that the world swears is impossible.

When the church becomes a PAC, it loses exactly this. It sorts itself by the same lines that sort everyone else, and so it has nothing to say that the world has not already said. It gains a little temporary access and surrenders its entire reason for existing. A church captured by a party can no longer call that party to account, can no longer welcome the person on the other side, can no longer be the one place in a fractured country where the fracture does not run. It trades the new humanity for a mailing list. This does not mean the church is silent on justice. It means the church speaks as the church, naming sin wherever it appears and refusing to launder the sins of one tribe while condemning the other. A prophet who only ever indicts the other side is not a prophet. He is a partisan with a Bible.

The church that keeps its nerve will frustrate everyone who wants to use it. The activists will find it too slow, too unwilling to deliver the bloc. The partisans will find it too willing to name their own side's failures. Good. That frustration is the evidence that it is still the church and not yet a tool. Its job is to form people whose loyalties are so reordered that they cannot be fully captured by any faction, and then to release those people into the world as citizens who carry that reordering with them into the booth, the council meeting, the argument with a neighbor over the fence.

sections.title: Faithful Presence
sections.body:
James Davison Hunter gave us a phrase for what is left when the dreams of conquest fall away. Faithful presence. It is not a strategy to win the culture. It is a way of being in it. It says the calling of the Christian is to be fully present, faithful, and committed within his actual place, his real relationships, his particular corner of the world, and to seek the good of the people there whether or not it ever scales into national change. It is unglamorous. It does not trend. It is also the only thing that has ever made the kingdom believable to people who were not arguing about it.

Think about what this means on a Tuesday. It means loving the neighbor you actually have, the one across the street whose politics make your jaw tighten, not the abstract neighbor in your feed who agrees with you. It means telling the truth when a lie would be more useful to your side, and telling it even about your side. It means serving the poor not as a policy position you hold but as people you know by name, whose troubles cost you something. It means showing up for the long, local, repetitive work of a place, the meetings and the meals and the funerals, where reputation is built slowly and trust is the only currency that finally moves anything. Newbigin, after a lifetime as a missionary, said the only hermeneutic of the gospel that the world finds convincing is a congregation of men and women who live by it. Not an argument. A people.

This is the patience the moment demands and the patience the moment hates. Everything in the political machinery is built to make you believe the next election is the last one, that this cycle is the apocalypse, that you must give it everything because the world ends if you lose. The Christian, holding the longer story, can refuse that fever without refusing the work. He can labor for justice while knowing his labor is a seed and not the harvest, that he plants what he will not see grow, that faithfulness and not results is the thing he was actually asked for. This frees him to do the slow things, the things that do not pay off by November, the building of a life and a community that simply tells the truth about what human beings are for.

So render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Pay the tax, vote the conscience, honor the office, do the civic work with your whole strength. But know the limit of it, and know it in your bones. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get the image. The image of God on the person across the street, on the one who votes against you, on the poor man the system forgot, on you, is rendered to God and to no one else. A Christian who has settled that question can walk into the wreckage of our politics without being made into a weapon by it, can love a country without worshiping it, can lose an election without losing his soul. The world is not waiting for the church to win. It is waiting, whether it knows it or not, for the church to be the church, in plain sight, where the light is good and the work is real.
